content: The general symptoms of meningioma include fatigue and loss of appetite. However, the specific clinical presentation of a meningioma is determined by the precise anatomical location of the tumor. Neuroblastomas located in the abdomen may present with abdominal distension and constipation. Neuroblastomas in the posterior mediastinum may cause symptoms such as dyspnea and cough. Metastatic neuroblastoma lesions in the bone marrow may manifest as bone pain and limping. Neuroblastomas located in the head and neck region may present with facial bruising and facial swelling. The initial symptoms of neuroblastoma are often nonspecific and may include fatigue and loss of appetite. As the disease progresses, symptoms depend on the tumor's location. For example, a tumor in the abdomen may cause a swollen belly and constipation, while a tumor in the chest may lead to breathing difficulties. Tumors pressing on the spinal cord can result in weakness and an inability to move or walk. A tumor in the head may cause the eyes to protrude outward and develop a blackened appearance due to pressure from behind. Because the early symptoms are often vague, approximately half of all neuroblastomas have already metastasized to other parts of the body by the time a diagnosis is made. The signs and symptoms of neuroblastoma vary widely depending on the tumor's origin and the extent of its spread. Common symptoms include irritability, fatigue, loss of appetite, and fever in infants. In young children, a swollen abdomen, abdominal pain, and reduced appetite are common. Bone pain, black eyes, bruising, and pale skin may also occur. Weakness, numbness, difficulty moving a body part, or trouble walking can result from spinal cord involvement. Horner's syndrome, characterized by drooping eyelids, unequal pupils, sweating, and red skin, may also be observed. Breathing difficulties can occur if the tumor is located in the chest. Fatigue, loss of appetite, fever, and joint pain are common early symptoms, making diagnosis challenging. Tumors in the abdomen may cause a swollen belly and constipation, while those in the chest can lead to breathing problems. Tumors pressing on the spinal cord may cause weakness, leading to an inability to stand, crawl, or walk. Bone lesions in the legs and hips may result in pain and limping. Tumors in the bones around the eyes or orbits may cause distinct bruising and swelling. Bone marrow infiltration can lead to pallor due to anemia. Neuroblastoma often spreads to other parts of the body before symptoms become apparent, with 50–60% of cases presenting with metastases at diagnosis. Clinical presentation typically includes pain, a palpable mass, and abdominal distension, although other presentations may occur due to the local mass effect.
